Antivirus programs are a dime a dozen these days, and while the vast array of security threats that assail modern devices can at times feel so overwhelming that protection seems impossible, a good antivirus solution remains essential.
Unfortunately, purchasing an antivirus can prove rather confusing. Companies offer a huge range of bundles with long lists of features, many of which are obscured in vague language. If you dig deep enough into a company’s website, however, you’ll find that most still offer the option to purchase the antivirus with few add-ons at a lower price. And if that’s what you want, Bitdefender’s Antivirus Plus is a good option.
Buying Bitdefender Antivirus Plus on its own is arguably a bit confusing, as the company strongly pushes shoppers toward more expensive and all-inclusive Bitdefender bundles, which include other features like a password manager , dark web monitoring, and lots more. In total, there are four different bundles to choose from: Total Security, Premium Security, Ultimate Security, and Ultimate Security Plus Extended, ranging from $60 up to $140 for the first year. There are also Family versions of these plans, which are more expensive but add protection for up to 25 devices and parental controls. All these bundles include the same antivirus protection, but if you search for Antivirus Plus on its own, though, you will find it . And it’s arguably worth seeking out, as Bitdefender's entry-level options are priced most aggressively.
Bitdefender Antivirus Plus currently offers an introductory price of $25 for the first year (and $50 after) for a single device or $30 for the first year ($70 after) for three devices. This is quite a bit less than Bitdefender Total Security, which is $60 for the first year (and $110 after) and only offers two benefits in exchange: a password manager and protection for up to five devices instead of just one. The lower tiers tend to be better deals, especially if you're after something specific.
That’s because Bitdefender’s pricing is most competitive at its lowest tiers, which may by itself be enough reason for many to choose it. Rivals like Norton Antivirus Standard, McAfee Essential, Avira Internet Security, and Malwarebytes Standard typically ask more for a similar level of service.
There is some variation here; Norton throws in a password manager at a lower price point, for instance, and some competitors have superior VPN service included (Bitdefender Antivirus Plus limits you to 200 MB of VPN data per day, which isn’t much). Still, Bitdefender Antivirus Plus is among the more affordable options, particularly if you’re more interested in the antivirus than the add-ons.
Savvy users might balk at paying at all, as many free antivirus options exist. Bitdefender itself offers a free antivirus download for both Windows and Android (but not macOS, iOS, or iPadOS). This is a fair choice, though it often means you’ll have to tolerate advertisements urging you to sign up.
Buying, downloading, and installing Bitdefender Antivirus Plus is a smooth experience. The payment portal is straightforward. The installer is really a downloader, so it’s a small file; the full download required by the installer is roughly 800 megabytes. Once the installation is finished, Antivirus Plus automatically runs an initial virus check. This took less than five minutes on a Microsoft Surface Laptop 7 running Windows 11.
Once installed, the Bitdefender Antivirus Plus interface provides a default dashboard that includes several common actions, including a quick scan, total system scan, and vulnerability scan (the latter looks for problems like a weak account password or an overly permissive network configuration). You’ll also find an option to turn on Bitdefender VPN, which is installed alongside the antivirus—though, as mentioned, you’re limited to 200 MB of data per day unless you upgrade to Bitdefender Premium VPN .
These features are largely standard for an antivirus program, though one extra feature requires more explanation: Safepay. This creates a sandboxed browsing environment meant to thwart threats like keyloggers and man-in-the-middle attacks. To be honest, I’m doubtful of the feature’s utility. I don’t believe these are the most common avenues cybercriminals use to obtain payment information; they’re far more likely to buy huge repositories of payment data stolen from compromised companies. It’s also rather clunky to launch Safepay for an online purchase, so I don’t think most people will want to use it.
I spent most of my time using Bitdefender Antivirus Plus on Windows, which I think is the best version of the software. The Android and iOS versions look largely similar to it, though of course compressed for a mobile device. However, macOS is the odd one out with an interface that looks different from its peers and, to my eyes, seems about five years out of date. It’s not terrible and has similar functionality, but I find this a bit odd. It seems like the macOS software is missing a software refresh that other platforms received.
A nice software interface is a perk but, at its core, antivirus software is supposed to stop viruses and other malware. So, how does Bitdefender Antivirus Plus rank?
Bitdefender scored well in AV-Test’s latest report , where it detected 100 percent of the tested attacks and received an AV-Test Top Product certification. It also received high marks from AV-Comparatives , which found it detected 99.5 percent of threats, enough to earn it the top three-star score. Bitdefender’s consumer products weren’t ranked in the latest SE Labs consumer antivirus report, but the small-business product detected 99 percent of threats and r eceived an AAA ranking in the April 2026 report .
The performance hit from Bitdefender Antivirus Plus wasn’t noticeable in typical use of either my Windows 11 laptop or my Apple MacBook Air M4. Bitdefender services consumed about 700 MB of memory in total on both platforms. That’s not a lot, and it's in line with what I often see from antivirus programs, though it’s also not trivial. I can imagine this could at times result in a performance hit on a device with 8 GB of RAM. My devices have 32 GB and 24 GB, respectively, however, so I didn’t encounter any issues.
Bitdefender Antivirus Plus checks off most boxes for an antivirus program. It’s affordable, easy to use, earns high marks from malware testing labs, and avoids significant performance issues when installed. But I do want to return to a problem I’ve mentioned before: the VPN.
Antivirus Plus advertises an included VPN. This is true, but it’s actually the free VPN service that anyone can obtain. The service has a strict 200-MB (per day, per device) data cap, which isn’t going to be enough if you want to use it as your main VPN. To be fair, Bitdefender does detail this limitation on its website—but it does seem like an added feature when, in reality, it’s available for free whether you buy Antivirus Plus or not.
You can, of course, subscribe to Bitdefender Premium VPN , but you must do so at full price. VPN Premium isn’t included until you upgrade to the Bitdefender Premium Security package, which is much more expensive at $80 for the first year (and $130 per year after).
That could steer you away from Bitdefender if you want an antivirus and VPN. Competitors like Norton and McAfee bundle an unlimited VPN service into lower tiers of service, which, though more expensive than Bitdefender Antivirus Plus, are less expensive than Bitdefender Antivirus Plus and Bitdefender Premium VPN combined.
Unfortunate VPN bundling aside, Bitdefender Antivirus Plus is a good choice if you want antivirus for Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS.

Böylece finans sektöründeki şirketler, ihtiyaç duydukları piyasa verilerine tek bir API aracılığıyla erişebiliyor.

The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Friday that Europe must not walk into Russian "traps" as it takes a seat at the table in talks to end the war in Ukraine, adding that a ceasefire is still the top priority. European representatives will be included in the next round of talks between Russia and Ukraine after being left out of Abu Dhabi negotiations earlier this week. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and US envoy Jared Kushner said Europe would join the next round of talks with Russia, as Vladimir Putin indicated Moscow will not compromise on its hardline demands to end almost five years of war.
In a packed day of shuttle diplomacy following negotiations in Abu Dhabi, Kushner and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff held over four hours of talks with Putin in the Kremlin before jetting to debrief Zelensky in Dublin. ⬇️
It ​is "extremely important" ​that Europe has a ​united ‌voice ⁠in ‌talks on Ukraine with ⁠Russia, Swedish Prime ​Minister ‌Ulf Kristersson said ‌on Friday, adding ​that he thought a variety ​of ​voices ​could benefit Russia ​instead of Ukraine.
The Kremlin ​said on Friday that Russia would ​be open to European countries taking part in Ukraine peace talks if ​it ‌saw that they ⁠were ready to contribute to the peace ‌process.
The comment suggests that Russia ⁠has not yet committed to including Europeans in the next ​round of talks, despite ‌US negotiators saying on Thursday that President Vladimir Putin had agreed to ‌their participation.
Asked if negotiations would resume ​in the near future with European representatives joining those from Ukraine, Russia ​and the US, Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters: "Once ​we understand their genuine intention and readiness ​to contribute to the peace process, then it will be possible to make a decision on holding ⁠dialogue on a Ukrainian settlement in ⁠an expanded format."
The Kremlin ​said on ​Friday that it is ready to carry out ​a ‌humanitarian operation ⁠to evacuate civilians from ‌the eastern Ukrainian city ⁠of Kostiantynivka, following a similar model to ​that used last month ‌in the town of Oleshky, if ‌it receives appropriate security ​guarantees.
In a call with reporters, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry ​Peskov called on the ​United States ​to use its influence ​with the Ukrainians to secure Kyiv's agreement to such an ⁠operation.

Estonian Prime ​Minister Kristen Michal said on ​Friday the European Union's representatives at the peace talks ​between ‌Russia and ⁠Ukraine could clearly be President of ‌Council Antonio Costa and Foreign Policy ⁠Chief Kaja Kallas.
"If we have to say ​that Europe should ‌be represented, then it's also clear that we have ‌people who have institutional accountability to ​people of Europe and also to our countries, these are ​Antonio Costa, and also ​Commission, and, ​for example, High Representative Kallas, so we ​have the persons to do it," he told reporters in Dublin before ⁠of an EU summit.

texts.https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckn8:
US envoys Jared Kushner (left) and Steve Witkoff (right) met Volodymyr Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening
Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia.
European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.
Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.
The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.
But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but there were no further details over how many prisoners would be exchanged or when it would happen.
US envoys meet Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Putin in Moscow
Europe's security 'fundamentally reshaped' by war in Ukraine
Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important."
He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it was to have European delegates "at the table".
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.
Earlier on Thursday, the EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, told the BBC's Newshour the presence of a European delegate showed the Kremlin "now realised that Europe is a big player".
Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.
Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin told a host of European leaders gathered in Dublin on Thursday that he believed the security of the region had been "fundamentally reshaped" by Russia's war.
"Many member states [of the EU] feel an existential threat because of what has happened in Ukraine and the potential, if Ukraine was to fall, for further aggression on the European continent," he told reporters.
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.
Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.
Earlier, the Ukrainian leader said that the military was facing more "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.
Starshield technology, which was developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX company for government and military use, has played a vital role in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

Decision disappoints experts hoping for world’s biggest emitter to take global lead on climate crisis
China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.
The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate .
Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”
China is in the midst of an economic transformation , from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.
Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year.
Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year .
The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.
Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.
“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said.
“They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”
It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.
After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor , the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.
The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.
China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues , setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.
Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C.
That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “ overshoot ”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.
India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.
The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand.
No decision on a host is likely to be made at this year’s Cop31 meeting , which is ongoing in Turkey, with the Turkish and Australian governments jointly presiding over the summit.

Russian president says he would target any foreign troops sent to Ukraine and refuses to soften territorial demands
Vladimir Putin warned US negotiators that Russia would target any foreign troops deployed to Ukraine, in a series of hardline remarks that came as the Ukrainian military faced renewed disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service.
During the talks at the Kremlin with the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on Thursday, the Russian president refused to soften his territorial demands, insisting on full control over four Ukrainian regions that Moscow claims to have annexed.
He also ruled out accepting the deployment of foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine , describing such a move as a “continuation of war”.
Putin’s comments appeared to severely dampen hopes that a peace deal could be within reach, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said there was a “window of opportunity” to reach an agreement before the end of 2026.
The latest trip to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, who have made numerous visits to Russia, was partly aimed at securing European participation in future negotiations, according to two people familiar with the talks.
Speaking after the meeting, Witkoff confirmed that European representatives would join the next round of talks. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he told reporters as he boarded a plane leaving Moscow.
The US envoys will now travel to Dublin, Ireland, where they will meet Zelenskyy and debrief him on the Moscow meeting.
Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, said national security adviser Jonathan Powell would join the talks in Berlin.
Amid a flurry of diplomatic activity, including the recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the Kremlin appears to have succeeded in reframing negotiations over the war in Ukraine as part of a broader discussion about European security.
But Europe is wary of Russian attempts to focus discussions on a European security architecture, while Moscow continues to pound Ukraine with bombs and missiles.
The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, told reporters: “We already have a European security architecture in place.” Kallas pointed to the cold war-era Helsinki accords and the Budapest memorandum , which guaranteed the territorial integrity of Ukraine. “The problem is that Russia is not keeping to those agreements, so right now the focus should be that Russia actually keeps to their obligations … and they don’t attack another country again.” Focusing on a European security architecture was a “distraction” without a ceasefire, she added.
Both Washington and Moscow have been urging European leaders to appoint a single representative to lead negotiations on their behalf.
“Once a representative is appointed, a chief negotiator authorised to speak on Europe’s behalf, there will be a four-way dialogue,” Putin said on Thursday.
EU leaders are due to discuss the issue of who speaks for Europe on Friday, but so far have declined to nominate one person to speak for the bloc. One EU official said the EU would be represented by its institutions when issues concerning the union were on the table, but played down any imminent appointment. They said: “Do I expect an agreement on a special representative? My answer is no, I don’t.”
Kallas suggested she – as the EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy – should represent the EU in talks, alongside António Costa, the president of the European Council.
More than 45 European leaders are meeting in Dublin for the European Political Community summit, a gathering that brings together nearly every country on the continent, apart from the leaders of Belarus and Russia.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, played down the importance of having a single European negotiator, saying “the content determines the format”. “There is no more US support. So there [are] some mediations, fine,” he said, referring to the process led by Kushner and Witkoff. “But at the end of the day we will be the one to define and decide for our future security as Europeans.”
The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said it was first necessary to get Putin to the negotiating table before deciding on a European envoy. Merz said: “It’s not about individuals. What matters is that Putin is prepared to hold talks.”
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy accused Musk’s Starlink satellite service of damaging Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian drone attacks, after Ukrainian military officials reported new restrictions on the system.
According to Zelenskyy, Starshield, a military version of Starlink funded by the Pentagon, has for several days been subject to speed limits of 100mph (161km/h) along the frontline and in Russian-occupied territory.
Similar restrictions last month prompted confusion over who had ordered them, with Musk and the Trump administration pointing fingers at each other before the service was partly restored.
The latest restrictions had made it harder for Ukrainian forces to intercept Russia’s increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy said, accusing the service of “helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine”.
Kyiv has contacted Washington to seek an explanation for the disruption, which Zelenskyy said appeared to be deliberate rather than a technical fault.

Google , Gemini 4 Hydrogen isimli yeni yapay zeka modelini tanıttı . Hız ve verimliliğe odaklanan model; kodlama, ajan tabanlı iş akışları ve günlük kullanım için geliştirildi. Gemini 4 Carbon ve Gemini 4 Argon daha uzun ve karmaşık akıl yürütme görevlerine odaklanırken Hydrogen , daha hızlı tamamlanması gereken görevlerde kullanılmak için tasarlandı.
Google, Hydrogen ile birlikte Gemini 4 ailesini daha geniş bir kullanıcı kitlesine de açıyor. Model; Google AI Studio , Gemini API, Gemini for Business , Gemini uygulaması ve Google Arama üzerinden kullanıma sunuluyor. Google AI Pro ve Ultra aboneleri ise Hydrogen'a Google Antigravity üzerinden de erişebiliyor. Gemini uygulamasındaki ücretsiz kullanıcılar modele, sistemin uygun gördüğü sorgularda otomatik model seçimi üzerinden erişebilecek.
Gemini 4 Hydrogen, önceki nesilde benzer bir konuma sahip olan Gemini 3.8 Flash' ın önemli bir yükseltmesi olarak öne çıkıyor. Google'ın paylaştığı verilere göre model, varsayılan yüksek düşünme seviyesinde görevleri Gemini 3.8 Flash'a kıyasla 2,5 kat daha hızlı tamamlıyor. Terminal-Bench 4.1 testindeki başarı oranı ise yüzde 18,2'den yüzde 57'ye çıkıyor.
Şirket ayrıca Hydrogen'ın gerçeğe dayanmayan iddialar üretme oranını beş kattan fazla azalttığını belirtiyor. Model, 1 milyon tokenlık girdi bağlam penceresini desteklerken 1 milyon tokene kadar çıktı üretebiliyor. Google'ın iş ortaklarıyla yaptığı ilk testlerde Hydrogen'ın Gemini 3.8 Flash 'a kıyasla 2 ila 2,8 kat daha hızlı çalıştığı, token kullanımını ise yüzde 12 ila yüzde 23 arasında azalttığı belirtiliyor. Model; büyük kod depolarını inceleme, hata ayıklama, veri analizi, araştırma ve çok modlu dosyalar üzerinde çalışma gibi görevler için de optimize edilmiş durumda.
Hydrogen'ın dikkat çeken özelliklerinden biri de farklı düşünme seviyeleri sunması. Modelde low, medium, high ve xhigh olmak üzere dört farklı düşünme seviyesi bulunuyor. Böylece geliştiriciler görevin karmaşıklığına göre hız, maliyet ve akıl yürütme kapasitesi arasında seçim yapabiliyor. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 'te Hydrogen, varsayılan high seviyesinde 51 puanla Gemini 4 Argon'un 50 puanlık sonucunu geçerken, xhigh seviyesinde 54 puana ulaşıyor .
Gemini 4 Hydrogen'ın fiyatlandırması, 1 milyon tokenlık bağlam penceresinin tamamında değişmeden uygulanıyor. Modelin API fiyatı 1 milyon girdi tokenı için 1,50 dolar, 1 milyon çıktı tokenı için ise 7,50 dolar olarak belirlendi.
Google, Hydrogen'ı tek başına kullanılabilecek bir model olmasının yanı sıra Carbon ve Argon ile birlikte çalışan çok modelli sistemlerin bir parçası olarak da konumlandırıyor. Şirket bu amaçla Google Antigravity'ye Orchestrator isimli yeni bir özellik ekledi. Orchestrator, aynı görev sırasında Carbon ve Hydrogen gibi farklı modeller arasında otomatik olarak geçiş yapabiliyor. Google'ın Terminal-Bench 4.0 testlerinde bu yaklaşım, Carbon'a yakın başarı oranı elde ederken ortalama yüzde 24 daha az kota kullandı ve görevleri yüzde 19 daha hızlı tamamladı.
Gemini 4 Hydrogen aynı zamanda Google Arama'daki AI Mode' un varsayılan modeli haline geliyor. Google, modelin çok parçalı soruları, yazım hatalarını ve ayrıntılı sorguları daha iyi anlayabildiğini; yanıtların daha görsel hale geleceğini ve kullanıcılara daha geniş bir kaynak yelpazesi sunulacağını belirtiyor. Hydrogen ayrıca AI Overviews' ta daha karmaşık sorular için kullanılacak. Gemini uygulamasında ise Hydrogen; talimatlara, tona ve istenen biçime daha sıkı bağlı kalacak şekilde geliştirildi.
Google'a göre model, e-posta taslakları, araştırmalar, metin düzenlemeleri ve belgelerde daha az ek yönlendirmeyle kullanıma hazır sonuçlar üretebiliyor. Aynı zamanda Gmail ve Google Drive gibi Google hizmetleri ile Airtable ve Dropbox gibi bağlı uygulamalardan gelen bilgileri kullanarak çok adımlı görevleri yerine getirebiliyor.
Google'ın birkaç gün içinde Gemini 4 Carbon'ın ardından Hydrogen'ı da kullanıma sunması, şirketin Gemini 4 ailesini tek bir genel amaçlı model yerine farklı hız, maliyet ve akıl yürütme ihtiyaçlarına göre ayrıştırmaya başladığını gösteriyor. Hydrogen bu yapıda özellikle yüksek hacimli günlük görevler ve ajan tabanlı iş akışları için daha ekonomik ve hızlı seçenek olarak konumlanıyor.

Pope Leo XIV met six victims of clerical abuse in Peru on Thursday, including people linked to disbanded group Sodalitium Christianae Vitae. The US-born pontiff also urged the Catholic Church to make amends to survivors and strengthen protections against abuse as he returned to the country where he served as a missionary and bishop for nearly two decades.
Pope Leo XIV met six victims of clerical abuse in Peru on Thursday, including some linked to the once-powerful and now-disbanded Catholic society, Sodalitium Christianae Vitae.
The US-born pope is on a nostalgic return to the nation he calls his "homeland", and knows the abuse scandal well from the nearly two decades he worked in Peru as a missionary and bishop.
Watch more ‘Peruvian pope’ Leo XIV comes home to a country that shaped his life and faith through 'hardship'
Leo spent over an hour with the victims, meeting "each person individually, listening to their stories of suffering and their pain", and "thanked them for their invaluable testimony", the Vatican said.
Together, "they reflected on how to foster a shift in mindset – by listening to victims, seeking the truth, pursuing paths towards healing, and committing to the creation of safe environments", it said.

Sodalitium Christianae Vitae (SCV), a lay society founded in the 1970s that was widespread in Latin America, was shut down in 2025 by Leo's predecessor Francis after years of allegations of sexual, physical and psychological abuse, as well as corruption.
Before he was elected Pope Leo XIV, Robert Francis Prevost was the bishop designated to hear from SCV victims, who said he was supportive of their claims.
In an address to bishops earlier Thursday, Leo described the "pain" caused by Catholic clerical abuse and said the Church must make "amends" to victims and foster "a culture of prevention and protection".
Clerical abuse, a global scourge, was "a reality that has caused us so much pain", the 71-year-old said.
In April 2026, the Vatican announced plans to set up a "listening channel" in Lima for victims, and use assets seized from the lay movement to compensate them.
Renzo Orbegozo, a 50-year-old victim, told AFP they were seeking "comprehensive reparation".
"Many require psychological and medical support, as well as social reintegration – all of which, ultimately, translates into financial assistance," he said.
On the eve of the pope's South America tour, the US -based non-profit Bishop Accountability presented a list in Lima of 77 members of the Peruvian clergy it said had been publicly accused of abusing minors.
Anne Barrett Doyle, co-director of the group, called on Leo to implement "zero tolerance" of abusers.
The head of the 1.4 billion Catholics has not shied away from tackling sensitive political and social topics during his three-nation Latin American tour.
Read more Pope Leo calls for healthcare to be 'accessible for all' during Uruguay visit
Pilgrim Pedro Campos said Leo was "a member of our country who ... knows the needs of all Peruvians."
At a speech later to some 40,000 people on the challenges facing Peruvians, the pontiff slammed "machismo" attitudes and said violence against women was "a reality that wounds all of humanity".
There was no excuse for "an unequal sharing of domestic responsibilities or the subordination of one spouse to the other", he said.
Read more Pope Leo urges men to respect wives amid Latin American femicide crisis
Chicago-born Leo was given a raucous reception by crowds lining the streets, chanting his name.
Thousands of people – including children dressed as the pope or as bishops – lined up for a glimpse of the pope as he drove by in the popemobile.
At a prayer vigil attended by some 60,000 young people in Lima's national stadium, the pope made his way around on foot to greet people, as thousands held up their phones as torches.
The intense trip to Uruguay , Argentina and Peru comes just weeks after the pope had surgery for lung cancer, but he shows no sign of flagging.
In his speech, Leo made fond references to Peru's landscape and culture, telling the Catholic clergy to think of their mission as a difficult but rewarding walk, like the path that leads to Machu Picchu.
He compared the Catholic mission to the "steep ascents" of the Inca Trail in Peru.
The trail, an ancient network of routes that traverses much of the Andes, "is not to be walked alone", he cautioned.
Read more Pope Leo XIV returns to second homeland Peru and a nationwide welcome
During his tenure in Peru, Prevost worked in poor and remote northern areas, and remained close to local communities during periods of hardship, visiting them sometimes on horseback.
Six days in Peru will see Leo travel from the deep Amazon to the high Andes. He will visit Cuzco, at more than 3,400 metres (11,000 feet) elevation, which will test his recovery from lung surgery.
He will also make an emotional return to Chiclayo, the northern city where he was bishop for a decade.

Overnight attacks reported on both sides as US efforts to broker a ceasefire struggle to make progress and Europe continues to ponder its role.
Russia and Ukraine have reported numerous overnight attacks, despite a diplomatic push to end the conflict.
Russian officials reported on Friday that a swarm of about 1,200 Ukrainian drones were fired at the country, with oil infrastructure among the targets. Ukraine reported that a hospital was struck and that strikes on the port of Odesa were ongoing.
The reports show that hostilities continue unabated despite the renewed effort of United States envoys to mediate a ceasefire.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence reported it had intercepted 1,198 Ukrainian drones overnight, across more than 15 regions.
Attacks in Volgograd in southern Russia killed four people as they hit an industrial area and left two others injured, regional Governor Andrei Bocharov said.
Volgograd is home to a major oil refinery, which unverified video posted on social media purported to show was on fire. There was no immediate official ⁠confirmation that the refinery had been attacked.
Ukraine has concentrated its fire this year on Russia’s oil infrastructure in a bid to cut off its earnings from energy exports, which are being used to power its ongoing invasion.
Sergei Sobyanin, mayor of Moscow, said 467 Ukrainian drones had hit the capital overnight, according to the RIA Novosti news agency.
Ukraine reported that Russian forces had been attacking the southern port city of Odesa since early on Friday morning. The city’s military administration reported that at least two people had been killed.
The Russian Defence Ministry said it had targeted a cargo ship in the Black Sea that was transporting weapons and military equipment for Ukrainian forces, according to the TASS news agency.
Ukrainian emergency officials reported six people injured in Russian attacks in the southeastern Zaporizhia district.
A hospital in Kyiv caught fire overnight after being struck during a Russian drone attack, leaving one person injured.
Reporting from the hospital, Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said the building was hit at about 3am local time (01:00GMT) and was severely damaged.
“This is a hospital that treats civilians, it’s close to the centre of the city,” she said, noting that many people had been forced to evacuate their homes amid the strikes.
The attacks came amid the renewed diplomatic push by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators met in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday and Wednesday, reporting an agreement on a major prisoner exchange but no progress towards ending the war.
Territory and security guarantees remain crucial obstacles. Russia is reported to have repeated uncompromising demands, including its right to control the entirety of Ukraine’s Donbas region.
Unconfirmed reports also said it had made demands regarding wider European security, including calling for Finland to leave NATO and for the Western military alliance to pledge not to base troops in the Baltic region.
The US envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday, then briefed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin, before a meeting of European leaders in the Irish capital on Friday.
Kushner said late on Thursday that Putin has agreed to include Europe in the negotiations. “We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table,” he said.
“I think it is self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in Dublin.
However, Europe continues to struggle to coordinate its approach, with disagreement over naming a lead negotiator persisting before an expected return to talks between Russia and Ukraine next week. The Dublin summit is focused on resolving the issue.
In Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s MacAlpine said that the Ukrainians worry that Russia is using the move to include the Europeans in the talks to distract from its refusal to concede occupied territory.
However, Moscow on Friday afternoon stated that it has not yet agreed to include European mediators in the talks.
“Once we understand their real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

WIRED'ın incelediği şirket içi yazışmalara göre tartışma, uzun süredir Nvidia'da görev yapan bir mühendisin Huang istifa etmeden önce öneri kutusunda yayımladığı gönderiyle başladı. Mühendis, yönetim kurulundan karar almadan önce çalışanların görüşünü resmî olarak toplamasını ve yürütülen soruşturmanın bulgularını şirket içinde paylaşmasını istedi.
Huang'ın ayrılığının ardından gönderiye yapılan yorumların çoğu, kurucu CEO'nun geri dönmesi yönündeydi. Bazı çalışanlar Huang'ın Nvidia'ya katkılarını hatırlatarak kendisine ikinci bir şans verilmesini istedi. Bir çalışan da şirket geneline gönderdiği e-postada Huang'a desteğini açıkladı ve yönetim kurulundan ayrılık sürecine ilişkin daha şeffaf davranmasını talep etti. WIRED'a göre istifayı izleyen saatlerde yaklaşık 24 Nvidia çalışanı LinkedIn'de Huang'a destek veren paylaşımlar yaptı.
Daha önce aktardığımız üzere Nvidia yönetim kurulu, Huang’ın yabancı bir istihbarat faaliyetinin hedefi olduğu yönündeki haberlerin ardından 8 Kasım'da bağımsız bir soruşturma başlattı. Huang aynı gün çalışanlara gönderdiği e-postada evlilik dışı bir ilişki yaşadığını kabul ederek özür diledi. Daha sonra kendisine doğrudan bağlı bir Nvidia yöneticisiyle de ilişki yaşadığı iddiası basına yansıdı. Şirketi 1993'teki kuruluşundan bu yana yöneten Huang, yönetim kurulunun 12 Kasım'daki toplantısının ardından CEO'luk ve yönetim kurulu üyeliği dahil şirketteki görevlerinden ayrıldı. Nvidia, finans direktörü Colette Kress 'i geçici CEO, Harvey Jones 'u ise yönetim kurulu başkanı olarak atadı.
Nvidia ve Jones, çalışanların çağrısına ilişkin WIRED'ın yorum talebine haber yayımlandığı sırada yanıt vermemişti. Şirket, kalıcı CEO arayışında hem şirket içinden hem de dışarıdan adayları değerlendireceğini açıkladı.

US House Speaker Mike Johnson has said ⁠there is a ​growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang .
Huang stepped down after reports of a romantic relationship with a businesswoman whom US ⁠authorities suspect of spying for the Chinese government. The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions.
In the last week, representatives from both sides of the aisle have called for tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips; chips that could underpin China’s surging AI development.
Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are ⁠widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US ​has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips ‌because it wants its own companies to stay ahead in the race.
“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told ‌reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“
Congressional Republicans are keen to attach ​new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defense authorisation bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke to Reuters on the condition of anonymity.
This live blog is now closed – but if you’d like to read more on Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia, our latest report is here .

A 29-year-old man has been charged after seven women reported being sexually assaulted on the Huddersfield University campus over a 30 minute period.
West Yorkshire police said Sophan Akbash had been charged with nine counts of sexual assault and would appear at Leeds magistrates court on Friday. Security staff called officers to Huddersfield University on Tuesday evening after reports of a man approaching and sexually touching women on and near the campus, police said.
Officers said seven women had been sexually assaulted by a suspect between 6 and 6.30pm on Tuesday. The women “had made off” from a suspect “after he approached and grabbed at them”, police added.
On Friday, the force confirmed that Akbash, of Huddersfield, had been charged with nine counts of sexual assault.
Earlier this week, Det Insp Sarah Bradley of West Yorkshire police said: “We continue to work closely with our partners at the university to provide reassurance to students and staff, and remain fully committed to supporting victims and safeguarding those who live, study and work in Huddersfield.”
The university’s deputy vice-chancellor, Prof Tim Thornton, said on Wednesday: “We recognise that incidents of this nature are deeply concerning and we are providing wellbeing support to anyone affected.
“As a precaution, we have increased security patrols around campus and are encouraging all members of our community to make use of our SafeZone app, which provides direct access to emergency assistance, wellbeing support and our campus support and safety team. Barely a week after sweeping to a stunning midterm victory, Democrats have found themselves facing an altogether different battle, one within their own ranks.
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen has launched a challenge to Chuck Schumer, of New York, for the Senate’s top Democratic leadership post. Announcing his decision during an interview with MS Now last night, Van Hollen argued that last week’s midterm election results showed Americans wanted a fundamental change in Washington, and that Democrats needed new leadership in order to deliver that.
double quotation mark We saw a huge outburst of democracy on election day – red states, blue states, purple states – and it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption, his wars and his cruelty, it was also about a call for a larger change, to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favour of the very wealthy against working people, and it’s fuelled by a corrupt political system.
The call was to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual, and to do that, I think we need new leadership.”
His challenge came just days after Democrats secured control of the Senate, winning at least 55 seats in what has been a remarkable election cycle for the party. Winning the leadership contest requires a majority of the caucus, about 28 or 29 senators, with an election scheduled for next month.
The caucus votes behind closed doors by secret ballot, but Van Hollen told MS Now that he had the support of “more than 10” Democratic senators.
Progressive heavyweight Bernie Sanders , an independent senator from Vermont who caucuses with the Democrats, has already publicly declared he will not support Schumer , saying “the time is now for change”. Endorsing Van Hollen, Sanders said : “The American people voted for change. They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families.”
Incoming Democratic senator Abdul El-Sayed, of Michigan, has also openly backed Van Hollen , saying he was “proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority”.
double quotation mark The American public spoke clearly last week. They rejected Trumpism. But we have yet to earn our mandate. That will require bold leadership. I called [Van Hollen] to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience. We need both right now.”
Responding to Van Hollen’s leadership bid , Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since January 2017, said he welcomed “a discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead”, but that he had the votes to be re-elected as leader.

Senator Chris Van Hollen , a Maryland Democrat, announced on Thursday that he is challenging Chuck Schumer for the role of Senate majority leader when Democrats regain the majority in January.
“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies – but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement posted on social media. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”

The battle pits a progressive Democrat, Van Hollen, against a centrist, Schumer, in the wake of Senate wins for progressive Democrats in Michigan and Maine who were not initially supported by Schumer.

Schumer is a cautious politician who has been widely criticized by Democratic voters for failing to stand up to Trump. Van Hollen, by contrast, took on the president’s mass deportation effort head on when he visited El Salvador in early 2025 and demanded to check on the condition of Kilmar Ábrego , a constituent who was wrongly deported to the country.

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed , the Michigan Democrat who saw off Schumer’s preferred candidate in the primary, quickly endorsed Van Hollen.

Standing in the yard as smoke billowed from the burning building, and firefighters led dazed patients to safety, one witness, Oleksandr, said the attack had narrowly missed patients. “We were asleep when there was this massive boom. We all jumped out of bed straight away.
“There was glass all over the floor. People were running about … If it had hit a little further to the left it would have been much worse. We felt the shock wave.”
He added: “Targeting the wounded – that’s really low. Russia attacks everything. Where I live, high-rise blocks are being constantly hit by bombs. They don’t care where they drop them, or where they land.”
Russia has recently stepped up its strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, hitting power plants, passenger trains and two bridges across the Dnipro river. Ukraine says the attacks are part of a campaign of terror, designed to make a weary population capitulate.
On Thursday, Zelenskyy said the Starshield system – operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and overseen by the Pentagon – was again experiencing significant disruptions, after an unexplained slowdown last month.
He said some Russian aerial sorties had got through because Ukrainian interceptor systems that rely on the US satellite service could not reach the necessary speed to knock out enemy drones. Starshield is the Ukrainian military’s version of Starlink.
The White House has yet to explain why the service has been throttled for a second time, but it comes after intense US-led shuttle diplomacy this week, with Donald Trump seemingly pressuring Zelenskyy to make territorial concessions to Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.
Trump’s emissaries, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and real estate developer Steve Witkoff, met Putin in Moscow on Thursday. They then flew to Dublin to brief Zelenskyy on their talks, which came after trilateral negotiations on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi.
Kremlin negotiators insist that Ukraine hand over four Ukrainian provinces, including cities and villages Russian troops have been unable to conquer. They are also calling for a new “security architecture” in Europe – a demand in effect that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture, before eastern European nations joined the alliance.
At the same time, Moscow does not want European states to be involved in US-brokered talks to end the war in Ukraine. On Thursday, France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, said Europe had to take part since “US support” for Kyiv had ended.
“Without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine,” Macron said. “At the end of the day, we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans.”
Meanwhile, Russian strikes ⁠on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ⁠overnight caused ⁠power ​outages in 12 ⁠regions, said deputy energy minister Artem ⁠Nekrasov. The ‌affected regions are ‌Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Zhytomyr, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Rivne, Sumy, Kharkiv, ‌Khmelnytskyi and Chernihiv.
“Energy workers ​are working at an intensified pace, ⁠but new attacks ​and constant ​air raid ​alerts ​are ‌complicating and delaying ​repairs,” ​Nekrasov said.
In Kyiv, the orthopaedic hospital’s director, Ronan Derkach, said medical services had been temporarily suspended as a clean up operation got under way. Thirty patients were taken to safety.

Young people are being found with ‘hard drives full of what can only be described as gore’, one expert says
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
In March, Guardian Australia revealed that most people who have been charged with the new federal crime of possession of violent extremist material are under 18.
This week Australian federal police sounded the alarm about a surge in teen extremism: 32 of the 37 young people prosecuted in counter-terrorism cases since 2020 were charged in the past two years.
The growth in youth extremism is happening within a sprawling online ecosystem. My investigations have tracked the rise of online networks that urge violence and nihilism for their own sake, in which perpetrators coerce victims not much younger than themselves to commit brutal and degrading acts.
In a review of 55 youth terrorism cases, the AFP has found that the profile is mixed. They are often young men. Many have received some support or intervention for a mental health condition. Some are from stable homes, others not.
What they have most in common is that they are young people on the internet. Experts say the age of those caught up in these crimes is decreasing.
In the last month two teenagers in Darwin have been charged with collecting documents that could facilitate acts of terrorism.
The arrests came five months after another NT teenager was charged with making posts with “pro-Nazi, anti-immigration, anti-trans and white nationalist themes”. The charge sheet alleges he also possessed videos of white nationalist terrorist attacks, including the 2019 Christchurch mosque shooting and the 2022 Buffalo shooting that it partly inspired.
Experts involved in harm prevention programs, including the Victoria University professor Debra Smith, have watched the age of this cohort decrease dramatically over the past decade.
Instead of considering the challenge exclusively through the lens of radicalisation, Smith says we need to recognise that some young people are being socialised and finding identity in online spaces that may appear exciting and transgressive but are ultimately harmful to themselves, and may encourage them to do harm to others.
She has seen cases where teenagers are being found with “hard drives full of what can only be described as gore”.
“It’s like getting involved in any other … unhealthy subcultural aspect of life … [such as] gangs or crime for payment,” she says. “There’s this offering of what young people can look at and get involved in that just simply wasn’t there years ago.”
The Guardian’s investigation into the growth of extremist material charges, as well as the surge of young people in Australia ensnared in sadistic online extortion and gore networks , reveals an amorphous online ecosystem in which young people may easily come into contact with extreme and violent content.
A teenager in New South Wales who pleaded guilty to possessing violent extremist material, among other charges, described how he first came across such content on TikTok when he was 14 and sought validation by talking to others online. He used ChatGPT to research the Boston marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev as well as security arrangements at the Sydney Opera House. He was sentenced to a three-year community corrections order.
Others have told police how they became involved in so-called “gore” channels on Telegram, where more and more extreme footage – including of animal abuse – is traded.
Given the age of many involved, Levi West, a research fellow at the Australian National University, says they may be considered as much victims as perpetrators, which is a significant challenge for how authorities respond.
It’s important for parents, schools and others to think about what’s sitting underneath the uptick in numbers, he says, and not just the “algorithms”. He points to the legacies of Covid-19 and lockdowns as well as the presence of screens and digital technologies in the lives of young people.
“We are not going to arrest our way out of this problem,” West says.
With people as young as 13 before the courts, Australia must consider if authorities are taking the right approach and have the right resources for this challenge.
The Guardian’s investigation into the possession of extremist material charges in South Australia and around the country found that many of those who had been before the courts faced a range of health and social difficulties, including autism diagnoses and learning challenges – and raised questions about whether some young people understand a crime has been committed.
Smith has seen many young people caught up in these activities who come from troubled family backgrounds, while others have had every opportunity in life.
There is a role for everyone involved in caring for young people, she says, from parents and schools to sporting clubs, to recognise when someone might be engaging in harmful behaviours long before there is a risk of violence, then help them access non-punitive pathways for help.
“It’s really important to understand it through a developmental lens – that these are young people who are making decisions with young brains,” Smith says.
“My grave concern is that if we are just giving everyone terrorism offences at [age] 12, 13, 14, 15, we’re starting to label them the thing that they will become.”
This article was amended post-publication for legal reasons.

A seat at the table for Europe now appears likely following comments by a US envoy who just held talks with Putin. But who will take that seat remains unclear.
European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.
When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.
The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi , followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy .
Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.
Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine , alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz insisted Europe will be present.
"At the table must be sitting Ukraine, must be sitting the Europeans, must be sitting the Americans, and naturally Russia," he told reporters in Dublin.
But he, like many other leaders, played down the idea of appointing a special envoy for the talks.
Zelenskyy is insistent on European involvement in the peace talks.
"Not directly yet, and not yet when the Russians are at the table," he told the other leaders during the Dublin meetings. "But Europeans are already involved. And we need to make sure that Europe becomes a regular part of these negotiations."
Europe’s division over exactly who should be present has caused a public battle to erupt. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote an excoriating letter to Costa last week, bemoaning the lack of unity.
"By projecting the image of a Europe that is in disarray, we are merely serving the interests of those who want this war to continue," wrote Meloni.
European leaders had even seemed divided over their level of frustration about the situation.
Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Jansa said in Dublin that it was creating a "bad mood" among leaders, however Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs disputed those comments saying, "I don’t feel that."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The palpable fear among the leaders in Dublin is that the US will accept Russia's demands that Europe changes the way it structures its own security, mainly through the NATO military alliance, in exchange for a seat at the table.
Putin said a commitment that Ukraine will never join NATO and even the potential rolling back of the alliance to remove new joiners Finland and Sweden , could be among his demands.
"What do we hear from them [Europeans]?" asked Putin during the meeting with Kushner and Witkoff in Moscow. "That once a peace agreement is signed, they will immediately deploy troops in Ukraine. This is a legitimate target for us, so the war will resume immediately."
This is exactly the kind of rhetoric the European leaders say they are most wary of , especially those in Russia’s direct neighborhood.
"Right now, we are in the [Russian] trap," said Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal. "If something is a threat to you, will you discuss your defense with the threat [itself]?"
US President Donald Trump said publicly that he was hoping for a "very big, beautiful agreement" that "might involve all of Europe."
Many of Europe's leaders speaking in Dublin referenced previous agreements with Russia that they believe Moscow has breached.
They include the 1975 Helsinki Accords, the 1990 Paris Charter, 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act and the one they consider most important: the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which forbids Russia from using force against Ukraine unless in self-defense.
The rancor over the seat at the peace talks is drawing focus away from arguably the bigger battle in the EU now ― how to fund Ukraine as the war continues.
Back in October, the European Commission identified a €70 billion hole in the EU’s funding it had promised for Ukraine’s economy.
Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico has opposed any further financial and military support for Ukraine.
But Germany's Merz warned he could block the EU's next seven-year budget unless member states agree to contribute to Ukraine's financing.
